claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is governed by a two-stage mechanism.
Initial deformation is dominated by dislocation nucleation localized at nanoscale interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion and local short-range order enhance interface-localized dislocation nucleation.
With time, the interfaces facilitate a transition from dislocation nucleation to diffusion-mediated dislocation climb.
Interface-mediated evolution permits gradual plastic deformation while preserving nanoscale multilayer integrity.
The starting FCC/BCC HEA multilayers possess severe lattice distortion and established short-range order.
Sustained stress and elevated temperature can induce creep in a high-entropy alloy system.
Sharp and graded interfaces modulate interface energy and lattice misfit.
Interface characteristics affect dislocation-mediated deformation in HEA-containing nanolaminates.
Compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range order concentrate local stress at multilayer interfaces.
The initial elastic regime gives way to dislocation nucleation at heterogeneous interfaces.
Dislocations subsequently climb through localized atomic diffusion during sustained loading.
The distorted lattice environment aids localized atomic diffusion.
Sustained loading will produce increasing dislocation density and local interface rearrangements.
The sustained-loading state will exhibit greater interface diffusional activity than the as-deposited or short-term-loaded baseline.
Creep strain will increase with loading time.
The proposed behavior occurs only while nanoscale multilayer morphology remains preserved and loading remains below catastrophic interface-failure or delamination conditions.
Creep behavior should correlate with engineered interface characteristics and differ between sharp-interface and graded-interface multilayers.
